extracted.intended_audience: credit card issuers, compliance officers, and regulatory counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and compliance guidance for §1026.52 (penalty and prohibited fees) under Regulation Z; explains what costs, timing, dollar-limits, safe harbors, and prohibitions apply to late fees, returned payment fees, over‑the‑limit fees, declined access check fees, inactivity/closed-account fees, and related examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs incurred as a result of returned payments
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of §1026.52(b)(1)(i), the costs incurred by a card issuer as a result of returned payments are the costs the issuer reasonably associates with returned-payment events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and guidance include: using past costs to calculate a reasonable fee (example: a $27 returned payment fee representing a reasonable proportion of total returned-payment costs in year two), adjusting for inability to collect some fees, and adjusting based on reasonable estimates of future changes in costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs incurred as a result of over-the-limit transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of §1026.52(b)(1)(i), the costs incurred by a card issuer as a result of over-the-limit transactions include costs associated with determining whether to authorize over-the-limit transactions and costs associated with notifying the consumer that the credit limit has been exceeded and arranging for payments to reduce the balance below the credit limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples: (A) fee based on past fees and costs (e.g., $23 fee given certain historical authorizations and costs); (B) adjust when issuer unable to collect a portion of imposed fees (e.g., 30% uncollected leads to higher per-collected-fee amount); (C) adjust based on reasonable estimates of future transaction and collection rates and expected changes in costs (example: $30 fee after estimating same authorization counts but 6% decrease in costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs not incurred as a result of over-the-limit transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs associated with obtaining the affirmative consent of consumers to the card issuer's payment of transactions that exceed the credit limit consistent with §1026.56 are not costs incurred by a card issuer as a result of over-the-limit transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exclusion means costs of securing consent under §1026.56 cannot be included in the cost base for calculating over-the-limit fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs incurred as a result of declined access checks
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of §1026.52(b)(1)(i), costs incurred by a card issuer as a result of declining payment on an access check include: (A) costs associated with determining whether to decline payment, (B) costs processing declined checks and reconciling systems, (C) costs investigating potential fraud, and (D) costs notifying the consumer and merchant or other party that payment was declined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If issuer declined 100,000 access checks and incurred $2 million in costs and was unable to collect 10% of fees, a $22 declined access check fee could represent a reasonable proportion of costs during year two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe-harbor for multiple violations of same type (§1026.52(b)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A card issuer (other than a smaller card issuer) cannot impose a late fee in excess of $8 pursuant to §1026.52(b)(1)(ii), regardless of whether the issuer has imposed a late fee within the six previous billing cycles. For other penalty fees, an issuer cannot impose the higher subsequent-fee tier under (b)(1)(ii)(B) unless a fee was previously imposed for the same type under (b)(1)(ii)(A). Once a fee has been imposed under (A), the issuer may impose the (B) fee for subsequent violations of the same type until that violation type has not occurred for six consecutive complete billing cycles. A fee is considered imposed even if subsequently waived or rebated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The safe harbor creates a two-tier first/second+ violation structure, a 6-billing-cycle tail period, and treats waived fees as 'imposed' for the purposes of triggering subsequent higher fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing definitions for when specific violations occur
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of §1026.52(b)(1)(ii): (A) a late payment occurs during the billing cycle in which the payment may first be treated as late consistent with the account terms; (B) a returned payment occurs during the billing cycle in which the payment is returned to the issuer; (C) a transaction that exceeds the credit limit occurs during the billing cycle in which the transaction occurs or is authorized; (D) a declined access check is declined during the billing cycle in which the issuer declines payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These timing rules determine whether multiple violations fall within the 'same type' for the six-billing-cycle safe-harbor window and are used in examples throughout the guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship to §1026.56 and treatment of multiple violations based on same event
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple violations are based on the same event or transaction such that §1026.52(b)(2)(ii) prohibits imposing more than one fee, that event constitutes a single violation for purposes of §1026.52(b)(1)(ii). Also, no more than one violation for exceeding an account's credit limit can occur during a single billing cycle for purposes of §1026.52(b)(1)(ii), consistent with §1026.56(j)(1)(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, §1026.52(b)(2)(ii) does not prohibit imposition of fees for exceeding the credit limit in consecutive billing cycles if §1026.56(j)(1) permits those fees; in that case the second and third over-the-limit fees may be imposed pursuant to §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(B). Examples illustrate over-the-limit sequences and the interplay with §1026.56(j)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of safe-harbor application (same-type and different-type violations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous examples demonstrate application of §1026.52(b)(1)(ii) for over-the-limit occurrences, sequences across billing cycles, and interactions between different violation types (e.g., late payment and over-the-limit; late payment and returned payment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show when a higher subsequent fee may be imposed within six billing cycles, when only the lower fee applies because the later event falls outside the six-cycle window, and when only one fee is permitted because two outcomes stem from the same underlying event or transaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual CPI adjustments to safe-harbor penalty amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(A) and (B), the Bureau will calculate each year price level adjusted amounts using the Consumer Price Index in effect on June 1 of that year. When the cumulative change in the adjusted minimum value rises or falls by a whole dollar, the Bureau will increase or decrease those amounts by $1.00 and publish adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes historical threshold amounts for multiple years (2013–2024) showing prior permissible amounts under (A) and (B), e.g., $25/$35 (2013), $30/$41 (through May 13, 2024), etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delinquent balance rule for charge card accounts (§1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(C))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a charge card issuer that requires payment of outstanding balances in full has not received the required payment for two or more consecutive billing cycles, the issuer may impose a late payment fee that does not exceed three percent of the delinquent balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delinquent balance is any previously billed amount that remains unpaid at the time the late payment fee is imposed; the fee calculation may not include transactions from the current billing cycle. Examples illustrate computing 3% of the relevant previously-billed unpaid amount and alternative imposition of the $8 flat fee where permitted; cannot impose both §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(C) and (b)(1)(ii)(B) for same late payment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller card issuer exception for late fees
rubrics_metrics.description: A card issuer that meets the definition of 'smaller card issuer' in §1026.52(b)(3) may impose a fee for a late payment that does not exceed the amounts in §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(A) or (B), as applicable, notwithstanding the $8 late-fee limit for non-smaller issuers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: under historical thresholds, a smaller issuer could impose $25 for a first late-payment violation and $35 for a subsequent violation within the safe-harbor window, subject to other §1026.52(b)(2) limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited fees rule (§1026.52(b)(2)) — relationship to allowed fees
rubrics_metrics.description: A card issuer does not comply with §1026.52(b) if it imposes a fee that is inconsistent with the prohibitions in §1026.52(b)(2). Thus, the prohibitions in §1026.52(b)(2) apply even if a fee would otherwise be consistent with §1026.52(b)(1)(i) or (ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, even if (b)(1)(i) would allow a $27 fee based on cost-proportion, (b)(2)(i) prohibits imposing that fee if the dollar amount associated with the violation is less than $27; likewise a fee allowed by (b)(1)(ii) may be prohibited by (b)(2)(i) if the dollar amount associated with the violation is smaller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overarching rule: fees must not exceed dollar amount associated with the violation (§1026.52(b)(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.52(b)(2)(i) prohibits a card issuer from imposing a fee that exceeds the dollar amount associated with the violation; the guidance defines how to determine that dollar amount for different violation types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the umbrella principle; subsequent entries spell out the dollar-amount definitions and examples for each violation type (late payment, returned payment, over-the-limit, declined check, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dollar amount associated with a late payment
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of §1026.52(b)(2)(i), the dollar amount associated with a late payment is the amount of the required minimum periodic payment due immediately prior to assessment of the late payment fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: If $15 was the required minimum due on Sept 25 and no payment received, the late fee cannot exceed $15 even if (b)(1) would permit more. If partial payment was made, the relevant dollar amount is still the full required minimum that was due immediately prior, not the unpaid portion. If billing cycles close later and required minimum changes, the prior billing-cycle due amount governs for a late fee tied to the prior late occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dollar amount associated with a returned payment
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of §1026.52(b)(2)(i), the dollar amount associated with a returned payment is the amount of the required minimum periodic payment due immediately prior to the date on which the payment is returned to the card issuer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issuer may not impose a returned payment fee that exceeds that required-minimum amount. If a returned payment is resubmitted and returned again, there is no additional dollar amount associated with the subsequent return and the issuer may not impose an additional returned-payment fee for that subsequent return. Examples illustrate scenarios with different check-presentment and return dates, and which required minimum applies (the one immediately prior to the return). §1026.52(b)(2)(ii) also prohibits assessing both a late payment fee and a returned payment fee for the same event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dollar amount associated with over-the-limit fees
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of §1026.52(b)(2)(i), the dollar amount associated with extensions of credit in excess of the credit limit for an account is the total amount of credit extended by the card issuer in excess of the credit limit during the billing cycle in which the over-the-limit fee is imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus an over-the-limit fee cannot exceed the total dollar amount by which the issuer extended credit over the limit in that billing cycle. Examples: multiple small transactions that together exceed the limit produce a combined excess amount (e.g., $15) and the fee cannot exceed that amount. Nothing in §1026.52 permits a fee inconsistent with §1026.56 (affirmative-consent limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dollar amount associated with declining an access check
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of §1026.52(b)(2)(i), the dollar amount associated with declining payment on a check that accesses a credit card account is the amount of the check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a check that accesses a credit card account is declined, the issuer may not impose a fee that exceeds the amount of that check. Example: a declined $50 check means the fee cannot exceed $50. The fee must also comply with applicable (b)(1)(i) or (ii) limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on inactivity fees for open-end consumer credit plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.52(b)(2)(i)(B)(2) prohibits a card issuer from imposing a fee with respect to a credit card account under an open-end (not home-secured) consumer credit plan based on inactivity on that account (including failure to use the account for a particular number/dollar amount/type of transactions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a $50 fee for not using the card for $2,000 in purchases over a year is prohibited; imposing an annual fee on all accounts but waiving it for accounts used above a threshold and promoting the waiver to satisfy §1026.55(e) is prohibited. If the issuer does not promote the waiver, it may consider activity along with other individualized factors when deciding waivers or rebates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on closed-account fees and post-closure fee increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.52(b)(2)(i)(B)(3) prohibits imposing a fee based on the closure or termination of an account, including (i) a one-time fee to consumers who close their accounts, (ii) imposing a periodic fee after an account is closed if that fee was not imposed prior to closure, and (iii) increasing a periodic fee after an account is closed or terminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An issuer may continue to impose a periodic fee that was imposed before closure, but may not start or increase such fees after closure even if disclosed earlier. See also related comment cross-references (e.g., comment 55(d)-1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on declined-transaction fees when no dollar-amount is associated
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.52(b)(2)(i)(B)(1) states issuers must not impose a fee when there is no dollar amount associated with the violation, such as for transactions that the issuer declines to authorize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special rule for hybrid prepaid-credit cards: if an attempted access to the covered separate credit feature is declined, the issuer may not impose a declined-transaction fee either on the credit feature or the asset feature; fees for declines that would only access the asset feature (and not the covered separate credit feature) are not covered by this prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on imposing multiple fees for the same event or transaction (§1026.52(b)(2)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.52(b)(2)(ii) prohibits a card issuer from imposing more than one fee for violating the terms or other requirements of an account based on a single event or transaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If §1026.56(j)(1) permits fees in consecutive billing cycles based on the same over-the-limit transaction, those fees are not considered based on a single event for purposes of this prohibition. Numerous examples show scenarios (e.g., returned check that also causes a late payment) where only one fee may be imposed and scenarios where different events permit multiple fees (e.g., a late payment plus a later over-the-limit transaction in different billing cycles).
